query: Earlier efforts have produced HfNbTiVAl10 with a hierarchical heterostructure featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations and have used thermophysical-parameter calculations, CALPHAD, first-principles calculations, and machine-learning modeling to identify promising alloys. However, large computational demands and low efficiency impede rapid discovery, while fracture properties such as toughness remain difficult to predict. For HfNbTiVAl10 in its reported hierarchical-heterostructured state, what single testable methodological hypothesis could overcome these limitations for predicting Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness under tensile and fracture testing? Explain the rationale, quantify the expected gains in accuracy and efficiency over prior methods, specify the conditions under which it would cease to be reliable, identify supporting prior evidence, and define a blinded prospective benchmark that would decisively falsify it.

generation.boundary: The model's accuracy may decrease for predictions made outside the range of the training data, such as for different processing conditions or testing protocols
generation.uncertainty: The uncertainty of the prediction depends on the quality and diversity of the training data, as well as the complexity of the relationships between the composition, processing conditions, and mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys

falsification_experiment.design: A blinded prospective benchmarking study, where the machine learning model is trained on a dataset of high-entropy alloys and then used to predict the mechanical properties of HfNbTiVAl10 under tensile and fracture testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the machine learning model's predictions are not within 10% of the experimentally measured values for at least two of the three mechanical properties, the hypothesis is falsified

## Abstract
AbstractHerein, AlCoFeNiTi high-entropy alloy (HEA) samples were prepared by mechanical alloying using high ball-to-powder (BtP) ratios to investigate the effects of this method on phase formation, magnetic properties, and electrical conductivity. X-ray diffraction revealed that the prepared samples contained amorphous, body-centered cubic (BCC), and face-centered cubic (FCC) phases. The samples were dominated by the amorphous phase, indicating the influence of high BtP ratios on their structure. All the samples exhibited semihard magnetic properties, with the saturation magnetization (M s) value depending on the milling time. The sample synthesized at a milling time of 30 h exhibited the highest M s value of 60.1 emu g–1. The switching field distribution was employed to clarify the contributions of the BCC, FCC, and amorphous phases to the magnetic properties. The results showed that the BCC and amorphous phases contributed to over 95% of the sample magnetism, of which approximately 75% was attributed to the BCC phase. Notably, the magnetic properties of amorphous AlCoFeNiTi HEAs were demonstrated for the first time in this study.
